patient.chief_complaint: Found confused and combative at home, large GI bleed, hypotension
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W. is a 58-year-old man with severe alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD 22) who was found confused and combative in his home by his adult son, who called 911. He could not be aroused to follow commands and had large amounts of tarry black stool on his clothing. His son found empty vodka bottles — the patient had been drinking. On presentation, he is hypotensive (BP 96/58), tachycardic (HR 124), and febrile (37.8°C). He has prominent jaundice, caput medusae, large-volume ascites, fetor hepaticus, and bilateral spider angiomata — classic decompensated alcoholic liver disease. Melena on rectal exam confirms active upper GI bleed. His neurological exam shows GCS 10 with prominent asterixis, disorientation, and bilateral Babinski signs. His ammonia is 187 µmol/L — markedly elevated. He has classic HE precipitants: (1) active upper GI bleed (blood is a nitrogen load for gut bacteria → markedly elevated ammonia), (2) acute alcohol intake, and (3) possible infection (fever, tachycardia). EEG will show classic triphasic waves. CT head will be normal. This is a classic textbook straightforward HE presentation with multiple clear precipitants.

findings.morphology: Classic triphasic morphology: prominent positive phase 2, anterior-to-posterior phase lag present, bifrontal maximal amplitude, symmetric — TEXTBOOK HE triphasic waves

eeg.impression: Severely abnormal EEG showing classic grade 4 HE pattern: continuous generalized fronto-predominant triphasic waves at 1.5-2.5 Hz with anterior-to-posterior phase lag. This is the most characteristic EEG pattern of severe hepatic encephalopathy. No NCSE. Findings correlate with clinical grade 3-4 HE and ammonia 187 µmol/L. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy, grade 3-4, alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) — precipitated by upper GI bleed (variceal, nitrogen load) + acute alcohol intoxication (168 mg/dL) + spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (PMN 342)

differential.key_features: Ethanol 168 mg/dL — alcohol contributes; but ammonia 187 + classic EEG triphasic waves + ascites SBP point to HE as the primary pathophysiology; HE is the primary diagnosis
CT head no hemorrhage — despite INR 3.2; structural cause excluded
SBP confirmed (PMN 342, E. coli) — infection is a second precipitant of HE; the combined ammonia load from GI bleed + SBP cytokine-mediated hepatic dysfunction = severe HE

optimal_actions.action: IV thiamine 500 mg BEFORE dextrose — hypoglycemia 58 in active alcoholic; Wernicke prophylaxis
CT head — exclude hemorrhage (INR 3.2, fall risk)
Labs — ammonia, LFTs, CBC, coags, toxicology, BUN (GI bleed marker)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia 187, ethanol 168, Hgb 7.8, BUN 64 — classic severe HE from GI bleed + alcohol
Classic fronto-predominant triphasic waves at 1.5-2.5 Hz — HE pattern confirmed; NCSE excluded

optimal_actions.action: Paracentesis — SBP confirmed PMN 342; ceftriaxone 2g IV + albumin 1.5 g/kg
optimal_actions.expected_finding: SBP is second HE precipitant — treat with ceftriaxone + albumin

optimal_actions.action: Lactulose enemas + rifaximin via NG tube; blood transfusion for GI bleed; endoscopy for variceal control
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia falling as GI bleed controlled

critical_actions: Upper GI bleed is the most important HE precipitant to control — each unit of blood in GI tract generates massive ammonia from bacterial protein degradation; endoscopy for variceal banding is urgent
Thiamine before dextrose — hypoglycemic alcoholic patient; Wernicke prophylaxis mandatory
SBP must always be excluded in cirrhotic with ascites + HE + fever — SBP confirmed PMN 342; antibiotics + albumin save lives
Lactulose enemas are preferred when patient cannot take oral medications — 300 mL enema q4-6h for grade 3-4 HE with impaired consciousness
contraindicated_actions: Dextrose before thiamine in alcoholic patient
Beta-blockers (propranolol) during active variceal hemorrhage with hypotension — hold propranolol until hemodynamically stable
NSAIDs — worsen renal function in hepatorenal syndrome risk
Protein restriction — outdated; does not improve HE
key_reasoning_points: Upper GI bleed is the most potent HE precipitant — blood in the colon is a massive nitrogen substrate for gut bacteria; BUN elevation (64) is a bedside marker of GI blood
Classic triphasic waves on EEG in the clinical context of cirrhosis + elevated ammonia = HE diagnosis confirmed; no further workup needed beyond standard management
Propranolol should be HELD during active variceal hemorrhage with hypotension — the chronotropic suppression prevents the compensatory tachycardia response needed during hemorrhagic shock
SBP coexists with GI bleed HE in ~30% of severe cases — always paracentese in any cirrhotic with ascites, fever, and HE

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute GCS 10 entirely to alcohol intoxication; treat conservatively and wait for ethanol to metabolize; miss HE and SBP
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ethanol 168 contributes but ammonia 187 + classic EEG triphasic waves + SBP confirmed = HE is the primary pathophysiology; alcohol intoxication at 168 mg/dL does not fully account for GCS 10 in a tolerant alcoholic; the asterixis and triphasic waves confirm HE

red_herrings.data_point: INR 3.2 (severe coagulopathy) suggesting intracranial hemorrhage risk
red_herrings.intended_effect: Focus exclusively on hemorrhage prevention; delay LP for SBP assessment due to coagulopathy; delay EEG while investigating structural cause
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: CT head first to exclude hemorrhage — negative; paracentesis is safe in Child-Pugh C with INR 3.2 when PMN diagnosis is needed (prophylactic FFP not required for diagnostic paracentesis per guidelines); EEG should not be delayed

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward HE: severe alcoholic cirrhosis, ammonia 187, classic triphasic waves on EEG, active variceal GI bleed as primary precipitant, SBP confirmed on paracentesis, acute alcohol intoxication — classic textbook Grade 3-4 HE presentation
